blocks.1: HENRIK WERGELAND IVAR AASEN P. CHR. ASBJØRNSEN ANNA ELISABETH WESTERLUND THE SHETLAND VOYAGERS BERGE VIKING THE TRAINING SHIP SØRLANDET CUTTY SARK RAGNAR THORSETH
blocks.3: In the summer of 1832 Henrik Wergeland was travelling in Western Norway. He came over the mountains from Eastern Norway, travelled out along the Sognefjord and on southwards. He stopped here for a time as a guest of Dean Dahl and was greatly impressed by the dean and all he had achieved here. Afterwards he wrote his well-known poem “Eivindvig”, which he sent to Dahl. Not many people can have received such a fine and mighty poem of tribute as thanks. The poem shows what feelings Wergeland, our beloved national poet, had for Dahl, and let it also stand as an expression of our thanks to this man of honour.
blocks.4: As is well known, Wergeland had roots in Verkland. In his book “Ei strilekrønike” (A chronicle of the strils), 1978, p. 110, Torolv Solheim says that Nikolai Wergeland's grandfather was baptised in Eivindvik church on New Year's Day 1725. On page 112 of the book he also says that Wergeland was related to the parish clerk's wife in Eivindvik. Here is the fine poem, quoted from the local history (translated from Wergeland's Danish):

blocks.55: During his study of the Norwegian language Ivar Aasen was here in 1843. He liked it here very much. In a letter of 11 June 1843, written in Bergen, to a friend, he says he stayed in Eivindvik longer than he had intended: “... I was there for eight weeks, the first two in Dean Dahl's house, where I had a good opportunity to use Icelandic books; the last six weeks I stayed with a farmer near the parsonage.” This letter appears in “Aasen – brev og dagbøker I” (letters and diaries) by Reidar Djupedal, pp. 68–71. Further on in the letter he writes: “In Eivindvig I was very well, and so far I have nowhere found myself as content as there.” The reason, he writes, “was the good acquaintances I had there.” Dahl showed great interest in his work. In addition to writings in Old Norse, he was able to borrow Haldorson's Icelandic dictionary from Dahl. He also mentions a “Candidate Foss” staying at the parsonage, “but my closest acquaintance was with a student, Niels Alstrup”, a farmer's son from the district who had been taught by Dahl for a long time and named after him, “and who is to go to the university this summer”. This was the son of the cantor Anders Furenæs, who lived in Fonnevik. He was a teacher together with his father from the age of 12 to 15, and then on his own until he was 22 (compare the local history on Fonnevik). He began studying for the priesthood in 1843, graduated in 1850 and was with Dahl for a time. In 1852 he was elected mayor, but already in 1853 he moved to Bergen.
blocks.56: Aasen also mentions a “schoolmaster Niels Clausen”, with whom he had daily contact at the farm where he lived. This was the son of Claus Jørgensen (Ytre Midtun) and is, as far as I can see, the same as the “schoolteacher Niels Klausen” who at the executive committee meeting of 15 January 1838 was appointed cashier and accountant for the “School and Poor Relief”. He was to work under the responsibility of his father (Claus Jørgensen) “until he has reached the full age of 25”. According to the local history, Claus Jørgensen moved to Åmdalsvik in 1819.
blocks.57: About the accountant's work, the minutes of the executive committee meeting go on to say: “The accounts must, under the penalty hitherto laid down by law, be closed and drawn up in lawful form and delivered to the executive committee before the end of March.” The sheriff Ole Jensen Utvær, shipowner, and “annex church cantor Torkild Jensen” were appointed auditors “for this year”.
blocks.58: Of those present at the meeting, only Dahl, Furenæs and C. Jørgensen signed with their own hand; the others signed “with the pen held for them”. Is this perhaps the very beginning of the system of municipal treasurers?
blocks.59: Another person Aasen had a great deal to do with here was Henrik Johnsen, Dahl's clerk. Johnsen later became a shop assistant in Bergen, and Aasen writes that of his friends in Bergen while he stayed there, Johnsen was “my closest”.
blocks.60: Ole J. Midtun has told me, from his grandfather Ola Jørgensen Midtun, that the farm where Aasen lived when he was here was holding no. 3 at Undertun. That it was at Undertun is also mentioned in Djupedal's books referred to above.
blocks.61: Aasen lived at the parsonage from 20 March to 3 April 1843, and then at Undertun until he left here on 13 May the same year. In his diary for 8 May he writes that he took a “sea bath”.
blocks.62: After Aasen had left, he kept in touch with his friends here, both by letter and through personal meetings in Bergen and elsewhere in the country.
blocks.63: He met Alstrup many times in Oslo; among other things Aasen spent several New Year's Eves with him. His diary for 30 October 1865 says: “Farewell to Alstrup”. That must have been when Alstrup left for Namsos, where he became parish priest in 1865. Later he was parish priest at Snåsa.
blocks.64: I will include one more passage from Aasen's letter: “As the common people of Eivindvig otherwise distinguish themselves by enlightenment and morality (to a great extent a fruit of Dean Dahl's persevering work for this cause, which has at times gone to extremes and brought him several unpleasantnesses), my stay in this district was the most pleasant I have had since the beginning of the journey; and my inquiries here were also made much easier; unfortunately there are not many places where one meets acquaintances who can be of any help in that respect.”
blocks.65: In his diary from the time after he left, Aasen writes one day that he had fallen “...into a gloomy state of mind; all the more so as I was now used to very pleasant company in Evindvig, where several gatherings with Dean Dahl, Candidate Foss and the student Alstrup, as well as daily contact with the schoolmaster Clausen and several other cheerful, decent people, had made my stay there exceedingly pleasant”.
blocks.67: In the book mentioned earlier, “Ei strilekrønike”, Torolv Solheim writes, p. 90, compare p. 150, that P. Chr. Asbjørnsen spent a pleasant summer evening by a bonfire in Eivindvik in 1855, listening to stories from “Bård i Skuggen” about his favourite subject – the strils (the people of the coast north of Bergen). I have heard nothing more about the visit of Asbjørnsen, the great collector of folk tales. Nor have I found out who “Bård i Skuggen” was or where he lived, but in “Norske Folkeeventyr II”, from p. 523 onwards, Asbjørnsen writes a good deal in “Fra Sognefjorden” about this colourful boatman. Bård must have come from Sogn, for Asbjørnsen writes that he told his tales in “his beautiful, ringing Sogn dialect”. Bård “knew everyone, and everyone knew him.”
blocks.69: As mentioned earlier, the clairvoyant Anna Elisabeth Westerlund was here in 1983. Her visit came about because Ivar Henriksbø learned that she had “seen” events from the saga age elsewhere. He thought I could contact her and get her to come here to “look at” the question of where the Gulating was, and after a decision by Gulen executive committee she came on Wednesday 6 April 1983. She stayed until Monday 11 April. The magazine “Allers” had a thorough report by the journalist Øyvind Kjølberg in no. 25 for 1983. Many newspapers also had journalists here and wrote about it. NRK was here too.
blocks.70: Although some of the material from the report to the executive committee after her visit has been used in various places above, I think it best to include here everything in the report that can be seen as an account of her stay.
blocks.71: On Thursday 7 April she went, together with people from the executive committee, the culture board, journalists and others, on an inspection in Eivindvik and at Flolid. On Saturday 9 April she was at Stemnebø. She stayed at Eivindvik Vertshus (the inn), and there she held “open house” every evening, answering questions. During her stay, in addition to those already mentioned, other possible places where the Gulating might have been held were also brought up and discussed.
blocks.72: Even before she left Oslo she saw the picture of the Gulating site clearly before her. On the way here, while they waited for the ferry at Leirvåg in Lindås, she drew her impression as a sketch on her drawing pad. Shortly after they came ashore and were on their way north in Gulen, she “saw” that they were approaching the right place. “Behind that mountain”, she said, pointing north. When she reached the spot where the road turned so that the mountain formations above Eivindvik came into view, she saw at once that the formations matched the picture she had within her, and the sketch. The driver (the journalist Kjølberg) had to stop the car, and she saw that here, “behind the hill above the sound” (Kirkeneset), was the right assembly site.
blocks.73: She had many details about the place; among other things she “saw” a road in the area, shaped in a kind of curve but ending in a straight stretch; she further “saw” a kind of stone pillar, a spring, streams, something of iron standing or partly lying there, a red house nearby, and a ravine leading from the mountain down to the assembly site. Not far away she “saw” the sea, and quays that seemed to run towards each other, and quays of irregular shape. Offshore lay an island. She also spoke of other buildings in the area. It was incredible how the details matched the place out by the municipal office building. The road is the road over to the former parsonage, which does indeed end in a straight stretch. The stone pillar is the cross at Krossteigen, the spring we know as St Olav's spring, there are streams there, one (now partly in a pipe) right in front of the place and one a little further west, on the east side of the old people's home, and the iron vision was connected with a wire fence that was partly lying down. The red house was there too: the storehouse by the former parsonage.
blocks.75: During the inspection we first drove in to the bend above the sports ground. That was where they had stopped the car when they arrived. She then followed her “vision” outwards. In the area by the old town hall she stopped the car, and there the “picture” matched the quays exactly. In addition, the shape of the steamer quay corresponds to what she had said about an irregular shape.
blocks.76: She had no doubt that the original Gulating stood in the area below the cross where the municipal office building now stands. This is the first site of a legal system. It was here that the assembly that survived, and gave the assembly its name, stood.
blocks.77: There has also been an ancient place of sacrifice in the area. She was so sure of her case that she thought further inspection was unnecessary as far as the location was concerned. No other place could match the details of the vision so completely.
blocks.78: From Krossteigen we went to Flolid. There has also been an old place of sacrifice and gathering here. The gatherings there were connected with the sacrifices and were marked by quarrels and settling scores by force. It was probably a kind of place of punishment where the local people settled disputes by force. The gatherings were very local in character, and the activity ceased around the year 1100, when the age of sacrifice came to an end. The gatherings had nothing to do with law and the legal system. The Gulating was not held here.
blocks.79: Besides visiting the place now called Tingvollane, she was strongly urged to walk around and look at other places at Flolid that might be candidate assembly sites, but she could not see that any of these places had anything to do with the Gulating.
blocks.80: On 9 April Westerlund was at Stemnebø. During the inspection, in a relaxed atmosphere, it was very interesting to wander around with Westerlund and listen to what she told about the place there, concentrating calmly on her “vision”.
blocks.81: Before we set out she had drawn a sketch of the area that figured in her picture of the historical events there. The most marked feature of her landscape was a cleft in the terrain, from the mountain down towards the sea. She said beforehand that she saw a lot of scrap iron lying around. On the sea in front of the place there had been much boat traffic in old times, and there had been important military activity here. There had been a watch station here, with a beacon watch as well.
blocks.82: When we arrived and walked eastwards along the shore, she explained where buildings had stood before, which the local guide, Otto Stemnebø, could confirm. Scrap iron lay scattered about. On a grassy bank a little up from the sea she “saw” that killings had taken place. Intruders came, and the watchmen found no other way out than to stab them. The bog down by the sea was then under water. In the hillock west of the cove there were old graves. The old graves were also confirmed by the local guide. His brother had found graves there long ago.
blocks.83: The hillock down towards the sea was formerly a small peninsula, and watchmen were posted there, but she “found” the greatest activity up along the cleft in the terrain mentioned earlier. Here the watchmen lived for short periods. They had simple shelters, hide tents, but later got more permanent, solid houses. There had been a weapon smithy in a hollow dug in the sand. The local guide could confirm that there was a hollow dug in the sand in the cleft.
blocks.84: She believed that in the Middle Ages this watch post at Stemnebø had developed into a fort, and remains of it may be found further up the cleft.
blocks.85: The greatest boat traffic was on the sea south of Stemnebø (Stemnebøosen), but there was also some traffic in the sound inside, which runs north–south (Nyhamarsundet/Folefotsundet), and the watch station at Stemnebø was responsible for controlling it. The watch station there was important “right from when Norway became Norway”, as she put it, and remained a military station into the Middle Ages.
blocks.86: She could not “see” anything suggesting there was an assembly at Stemnebø. No judgements were passed there; the only justice here was the military kind, when the watchmen had to intervene for reasons of security.
blocks.87: Other places that have figured in the debate as possible Gulating sites, besides those now mentioned (Stemnebø, Flolid, Eivindvik), were also, as mentioned earlier, brought up and discussed while Westerlund was here, but they were all considered out of the question.
blocks.89: On 8 April we were inside Gulen church and looked at the baptismal font and so on. (Only Westerlund, the journalist Kjølberg and I were present. Kjell Solheim came in for a short time and took some pictures.)
blocks.90: The first church here came as early as the 11th century, Westerlund says. It was a small, very simply built wooden church. It had an earth floor and hardly any seats; the people had to stand. The roof was also of wood, brown, probably tarred, boards. It was not a stave church. The church was very cold; people stood inside wearing lots of clothes. It had a small octagonal altar rail and a porch. The baptismal font also stood in this church. Westerlund cannot see that it was ever used for anything other than a font.
blocks.91: The first simple church was not well received by the people. They had difficulty accepting the new faith, and they damaged the church. Westerlund could not see clearly how they did this, but perhaps they set fire to it. When the church was destroyed, the font ended up outside, was neglected, and did not come back into the church until people, a long time later, found it again and came to appreciate using it again. The font is very old, probably from the 11th century. When it stood in the first, simple church, it was used as a base for a bowl that stood in the hollow of the font; the water was not put straight into the hollow. The bowl was probably of brass and was later hammered out into an octagonal dish. The dish was decorated with grooves and clusters. Westerlund cannot say for certain what became of the dish. It may have been destroyed in a fire, but it seems it was stolen and sold.
blocks.92: After the first church was destroyed, a new one was put up. It too was of wood. In this church there was heating, with glowing coals in iron pans. This church was looked after and improved; the earth floor was replaced with a wooden floor. It was altered after the Reformation. Later it fell more and more into decay and in the end was in poor condition; among other things Westerlund could see that the roof leaked. People worked hard to get a new church, and finally the church was pulled down and the church that stands today took its place. She believes that no more than these three churches have stood here.
blocks.93: While we sat in the church she told various things about the church, the priests who had been here and their struggle against immorality among the people. Some of the priests strove hard to raise morals, while others did not take their work so seriously, joined in and used the situation to their own advantage. They saw it as a job and tried to come out of it as well as possible themselves. Those who took their calling as a calling and tried to bring more order to things were often disliked, because the people felt they interfered too much in private life.
blocks.94: She began to tell of one who sacrificed much and threw himself very actively into work for the good of the district. After a while I realised it was Niels Griis Alstrup Dahl she was talking about. She cannot “see” names. When she had told a fair amount, she explained what he looked like. He had a pointed nose and pursed lips and looked very like Hans Nielsen Hauge.
blocks.95: I said that a picture hung down in the old town hall that was supposed to be of the man she was now talking about, but that there was some debate about whether the picture was of the right person. For I have heard that this picture of Dahl, as the first mayor of Gulen, had been swapped for a picture of someone else. She wanted to see the picture and said as soon as she saw it that this was indeed the right picture, and I must say that her description of the person beforehand agreed well with the picture. Since then people who know what Hans Nielsen Hauge looked like have confirmed to me that the picture is very like him.
blocks.96: Many gifts had been given to the church, Westerlund said, among other things for the organ and various furnishings. The altar cloth was unpaid work, perhaps given by an association. She “saw” busy hands at work on it. There were also gifts from well-known people. There was something special about two of the chandeliers; they are a special gift. I could confirm this about the chandeliers: the two hanging in the nave are, as is well known, a personal gift from Queen Maud and King Haakon VII.
blocks.98: We also came to the question of the third cross. Many claim that 3 crosses stood in Eivindvik. Asked about it, she replies that 3 crosses have stood here. What we call the third cross she believes was the one that came first. She could “see” that it was a little smaller than the other 2, was damaged and stood a little askew. The material for this cross, which was probably carved here, came from not very far away. She pointed in a direction north, a little east. This may fit Hyllestad, where stone similar to that of the other crosses is said to be found.
blocks.99: The cross was more simply made than the other two; it had only straight, square arms, no curves or hollows. When this cross came it aroused strong hostility among the people, who were used to the old Norse faith, and Westerlund believes the cross was vandalised. Later the cross was broken up further and used in a building – in a staircase or a wall. The house it was used in lies not far from here (we were sitting in the church when she told this); she pointed in a direction straight towards the house that Alfred Dingen now owns. (We could not see the house from where we were.) The house was yellowish brown, she said. (I have since been told that this house used to be that colour.)
blocks.100: The cross had stood in the slope above the churchyard (below Dingen's house), and remains of it could be seen on the outside of the house, she believed. We drove up to the house. The steps are now cast in concrete, but among the stones in front of the steps we saw some that may have been parts of a cross.
blocks.101: Westerlund believes that the two crosses standing today came from abroad. She thinks there was not much difference in time between the arrival of the 3 crosses. It was probably in the 11th century, and their raising had to do with the adoption of Christianity.
blocks.102: Westerlund could not “see” anything special connected with St Olav's spring, but the spring was there in the saga age too and was used during the assemblies. She believes the name comes from King Olav the Holy having quenched his thirst with the water there.
blocks.103: She believes that dwellings stood in under the rocky slope that runs east–west above the spring. Remains could be found there.
blocks.104: Asked whether anything could be dug up from the ground at the place she pointed out as the assembly site, she replied that she could not see anything now, but that a large wooden table had lain in the area. There were also logs to sit on at the table. There have also been sacrificial stones in the area.
blocks.106: At first the whole session took place in the open air; later came a covering of hide tents and then assembly buildings. She also “saw” the first cases brought before the assembly. There was a case of a neighbours' quarrel over a cow, and a case against a woman who was badly treated. The woman was treated cruelly and accused of witchcraft and infanticide. She was in her forties. The background was that she had been raped and had had a child that no longer lived. The woman was convicted. The man behind it went free. The judge was in his fifties; he was rich, quite a big shot. He was capable but probably could not write. Everything took place outdoors.
blocks.107: Westerlund was asked where Egil Skallagrimsson had his ships lying during the session at which the case between him and Berg-Onund was heard. She then drew a sketch, and this, together with her explanation, shows that it seems very likely that Egil had his ships lying ready in the cove north of Grønevika. The location fits well with what she explained about a power line and an undersea cable that now run quite near in the area. The statement that the king's men, when they went after Egil, did not see Egil's ships until they came out onto the Sogn Sea may also fit well with Egil having his ships somewhere near Grønevik.
blocks.108: On the day we were at Stemnebø, on the way back – there were 5 people on board the boat – Westerlund suddenly broke the silence by asking one of those sitting near her whether he had a small "peculiar" chest or casket that had held money, but he did not. She then turned to me, but I did not have a casket like the one she described either. “Are you sure you have nothing to do with such a casket?” Then I remembered the carved wooden casket that served as the bank's first cash box, which we now keep safely locked in the bank vault. This fitted the description she gave very well. The next day I took out the casket. Her description was quite accurate. I showed her the casket.
blocks.109: On Sunday 10 April she gave a very interesting talk at Eivindvik school, where a large crowd had gathered.
blocks.110: During the visit here several incidents came to light showing that her abilities are hard to explain away. The way she could pick out details was impressive, something many more than those of us here have experienced.
blocks.112: In the summer of 1977 a trip was arranged with a “convoy” of small boats from Måløy to Shetland, returning to Eivindvik. The trip was led by the harbour master Tønder in Måløy. They came to Eivindvik, half a day late because of a strong north wind, early one morning after a hard crossing of the North Sea. The participants first gathered at the school, and in the afternoon there was a gathering with a programme below the cross at Krossteigen, in front of the office building that had then been put up there. The mayor gave a greeting, and the school band, which had faithfully stood waiting on the quay until late the evening before, played. They had brought majorettes from Bømlo. Ivar Kleiva gave a talk on “The Gulating in our history”. People said it was a very successful event.

There was a gathering at the school with a programme and a briefing by Peder Lunde jr. about the boat and the voyage they were to make. Peder Lunde jr. was, until then, one of our best-known sailors. blocks.129: Ragnar Thorseth visited Eivindvik on 13–14 May 1991. Thorseth and his crew of 25 arrived here on the evening of 13 May in their 3 “Viking ships”, “Saga Siglar” (which had been here before), “Oseberg” and the new “Gaia”. The name “Gaia” means “Mother Earth” and was suggested by the President of Iceland, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir. With “Gaia” Thorseth was to sail via the Orkneys to Iceland and follow Leif Eriksson's course to Greenland, Canada and the U.S.A. The visit here marked the start of the voyage.
blocks.130: On Tuesday 14 May Fylkesbaatane's “Kommandøren” arrived with “prominent” guests from Bergen, “and from other cities of the wide world, consuls and we know not what”, as a report in the newspaper “Strilen” put it. Mayor Ola Byrknes brought greetings from the municipality. The mayor's speech was written on a parchment that was presented to Thorseth as a gift from Gulen municipality. In his speech the mayor said that Thorseth could hardly have found a more fitting place to start his voyage, for here in Gulen we truly stand on historic ground.
blocks.131: Many people had gathered on the quay. Those who wished could go aboard and look at the “Viking ships”. The school band played during the ceremony and Magnor Midtun read a prologue. The gathering ended with lunch aboard “Kommandøren”. In the afternoon the boats sailed south towards Bergen, and on the 17th of May itself the voyage went from there westwards across the sea.
blocks.132: This Tuesday we met “the old” and “the new” times together here in Eivindvik: the “Viking ships” showed us how the old Vikings came to the Gulating, and “Kommandøren” is the symbol of the most modern, fast and comfortable means of transport at sea.
blocks.133: It might be fun here to include what Bishop Neumann writes about travelling by “winged boat” in “Budstikken” nos. 47–53, 1824:
blocks.134: “one sits on cushioned benches around a little table, quite cosily, sees through the small windows the land glide past at every stroke of the oars, keeps the doors open for the fresh air to stream in in good weather, but closes them for protection against all the harm of bad weather when the rain pours down. There is no more comfortable way to travel, almost too comfortable.”
blocks.135: FROM THE WELCOME PROLOGUE FOR RAGNAR THORSETH
